opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think personalized PageRank was one of the choices we got most right, and it's also one where I'd be the first to point out its limitations.

The reason we went with it comes from the hippocampal indexing theory that inspired HippoRAG. The idea is that the hippocampus doesn't store memories itself. It stores an index of associations, and when you get a partial cue, activation spreads through that index to complete the pattern. Personalized PageRank is a very natural computational stand-in for that kind of pattern completion. You take the entities from the query, use them as seed nodes, put your probability mass there, and let it diffuse through the knowledge graph. The nodes that end up with high probability are the ones that are well connected to *all* of your query concepts, not just one of them. That is exactly what you want for multi-hop questions, where the answer passage might not mention the query entities directly but sits at the intersection of their neighborhoods.

What I like about it in practice is that it's cheap, it's a single retrieval step instead of iterative LLM calls like IRCoT, and it's very well understood mathematically. You don't have to train anything, and it gave us really substantial gains on multi-hop QA for a fraction of the cost of iterative methods. There's also some nice behavior from the node specificity weighting we added, which is a kind of IDF analogue, so very common entities don't wash out the signal.

Now the limitations. PPR is fundamentally a structural, context-free operation. Once you've seeded the graph, the propagation doesn't know anything about what the query is actually asking. It just follows edges. So if your graph has a lot of noisy or irrelevant triples near the seed nodes, mass leaks into places that are topologically close but semantically off. It's also heavily dependent on the quality of the entity linking at the start. If you pick the wrong seed nodes, PPR will faithfully spread activation from the wrong place.

A lot of what we did in HippoRAG 2 came from taking those weaknesses seriously. We brought passages into the graph as nodes alongside entities, we used dense retrieval to seed and weight things more intelligently, and we added a recognition-memory style filtering step where an LLM prunes the retrieved triples before they seed the PPR. So PPR is still doing the associative spreading, but it's operating on cleaner, more context-aware inputs.

So my overall assessment is that PPR is a great default for the associative part of memory. It's simple and principled, and it captures the "connect the dots" behavior surprisingly well. But it shouldn't be the only intelligence in the system. The interesting open question to me is whether we can make the traversal itself more query-aware without losing the efficiency that made PPR attractive in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says PPR is context-free and “just follows edges,” without using what the query is asking to guide propagation.

r002.rationale: It does not say that extending the random walks causes retrieval to favor globally popular nodes.

r003.rationale: It discusses noisy graph triples, but does not attribute benchmark performance to a scarcity of distractors.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Personalized PageRank is honestly one of the parts of HippoRAG I'm most happy about, and I think the reason is that it does something that's easy to describe but surprisingly hard to get from other retrieval methods.

The way to think about it is that we build a knowledge graph offline, where the nodes are the entities and concepts an LLM extracted from the passages, and the edges are the relations between them, plus some synonymy edges from the embedding model so that "Alzheimer's" and "Alzheimer's disease" end up connected. At query time, we pull out the named entities from the question, find their nodes in the graph, and then run personalized PageRank seeded on those nodes. So instead of the random walker restarting uniformly, it keeps restarting at the query entities, and the probability mass spreads out from there along the edges. Passages then get scored by how much of that mass lands on the entities they contain.

What that buys you is multi-hop retrieval in a single pass. If the question is about a professor at Stanford who works on Alzheimer's, a dense retriever has to hope some chunk mentions both things together. With PPR, mass flows from "Stanford" and from "Alzheimer's" and it piles up at nodes that are close to both, even if no single passage says both. That is the hippocampal index analogy we were going for: the index lets you complete a partial pattern and jump to the memory in one shot, rather than iterating.

I'd also say it's a very good fit because it's cheap and well understood. It's a sparse matrix operation, it runs in milliseconds, there are decades of intuition about it, and it has very few knobs. Compared to iterative retrieval methods like IRCoT that call the LLM each step, you get a lot of the multi-hop benefit at a fraction of the cost. And the two actually compose nicely; in the paper, putting HippoRAG inside an IRCoT loop gave further gains.

Now, the honest downsides. PPR is only as good as the graph, and the graph is only as good as the extraction. If the OpenIE step misses an entity or splits one concept into two nodes that never get linked, the mass just doesn't get there, and no amount of clever traversal fixes that. Entity linking at query time is the same story: if the NER on the question misses the key entity or picks a very generic one, you're seeding in the wrong place. We also found that highly connected hub nodes can soak up probability mass in ways that aren't semantically meaningful, so we had to weight by node specificity, which is basically an inverse-frequency idea, to keep "United States" from dominating everything.

The other thing I'd flag is that it's fundamentally an entity-centric view of the world. That's great for questions where the connecting thread is a set of named things. It's weaker when the relevant connection is abstract or relational, or when the right passage shares no entities with the question at all. So I wouldn't call PPR the final answer for graph traversal; I'd call it a strong, simple baseline that revealed how much you can get from single-step structured retrieval. Where I think the interesting future work is, is making the seeding and the graph itself smarter, and combining PPR with dense signals so you're not purely dependent on the extracted structure.

astra-6.text:
I think personalized PageRank is a very useful starting point because it gives us a way to balance the query with the broader structure of the graph. We start from entities associated with the query, and then relevance propagates through their connections. So retrieval can surface information that isn’t directly similar to the query but is connected to something relevant.

The particularly appealing part is that this can bring together evidence across multiple connections without requiring the language model to explicitly generate and execute each reasoning step. The graph traversal does some of that work for us.

But I wouldn’t equate it with reasoning. PageRank doesn’t really understand what a relationship means or whether traversing it is appropriate for a particular question. Its effectiveness depends on the quality of the graph and on identifying good starting entities. So I see it as an efficient, useful retrieval mechanism, with room for more query-aware traversal when the question requires a specific chain of relationships.

sol-6.1.text:
I think personalized PageRank is a very good fit for what we wanted HippoRAG to do. We start with the entities that are relevant to the query, and then we let activation spread through the graph. That gives us a way to connect information across passages without asking a language model to explicitly generate every intermediate retrieval step.

The personalization is important because we’re not just asking which nodes are important globally. We’re asking which nodes are important relative to the concepts in this particular question. And because PageRank aggregates across different paths, it can bring together evidence that you might miss if you retrieved each passage independently.

But I wouldn’t say it’s the final answer to graph traversal. It doesn’t really understand the semantics of each relation or whether a path represents a valid chain of reasoning. Its effectiveness also depends on the graph we build and the entities we identify in the query. So I see it as an efficient, useful retrieval mechanism that gives the language model better evidence, rather than as a reasoning algorithm by itself.
